title: An atom's weight
hookLine: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it (Quran 99:7–8)

lines: PEOPLE ARE SHOWN WHAT THEY DID.
cards: The ground moves. That's how the ninety-ninth surah of the Quran begins, the one called the Earthquake. The earth is shaken, and it throws up what it has been carrying.
A person looks at it and asks: what is the matter with her? On that day, the surah says, the earth tells her news. People come out in scattered groups to be shown what they did.
And it ends with two short, balanced lines: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of ill will see it.

teach.b: In this surah, the ground itself is a witness. The floor you walked on, the street you crossed, has been listening, and on that day it tells what happened on it. Nothing done anywhere goes unrecorded.
Pickthall's translation reads: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then."
The Arabic phrase is mithqala dharratin, the weight of a dharra, something tiny. Pickthall chose atom. Some readers picture a small ant, or a speck of dust floating in a sunbeam.
Either way, it's the smallest thing you can still name. The two verses mirror each other.

teach.h: SMALL GOOD AND SMALL ILL BOTH COUNT.
teach.b: Small harms count: the sharp word, the little lie. Small goods count just as surely: the held door, the returned text. For Muslims, nothing is too small to be seen by God.
In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells a companion not to look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face.
So the great question of death and judgment is answered here in the smallest unit there is. Not a grand gesture.
An atom's weight, done today, on ground that remembers.

how: Surah az-Zalzalah is short, and some Muslims recite it in daily prayer; Muslims recall its last two verses as a reason not to belittle small good deeds or small wrongs.

o: something tiny, the Quran's measure for the smallest deed
the scale where good and bad deeds are weighed at the end
an Arabic word for the earthquake that ends the world

games.q: what's inside the Earthquake — tap the pairs.
p: tells her news on that day
a good deed not to belittle

s: the surah says only great deeds will be seen
even an atom's weight of good or ill will be seen.
in this surah the earth itself tells what happened on it
on that day, the earth tells her news.
the verses only warn about bad deeds
they're balanced: good and ill alike will be seen.

games.q: you notice a small good you could do: a held door, a kind word. it seems too small to matter. what does the surah say?
o: skip it; small deeds don't count.
do it; an atom's weight of good will be seen.
games.why: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. a hadith adds: don't belittle even a cheerful face.

practice: Let your mind go over the next few hours and find a small good waiting there, so small it would be easy to skip: a message to someone who's alone, a dish washed that isn't yours, a cheerful face for a tired cashier.
Pick just one, keep it small, and picture it, and if you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Dharra, the Arabic word for something tiny, the Quran's picture of the smallest deed, good or ill, that every person will see. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, Quran 99:7–8: the weight of a tiny thing, an atom's weight.

carryVoice: Your line: ground that remembers. Nothing done, good or ill, is too small to count. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then.
